titular: Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster, cheaper model for Search and agents
resum: Gemini 4 Hydrogen replaces Gemini 3.8 Flash and is already in the Gemini app, Google Search and the developer API. Google says it is 2.5 times faster and charges $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.
per_que_importa: Small, cheap models are the ones millions of apps and search engines actually use, because every answer costs money. If prices fall, more companies can put AI into their products without costs soaring.

titular: Four nonprofits ask a judge to freeze the most advanced AI
resum: Public Citizen and three other organisations have sued Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI unit in a San Francisco court to stop them building or releasing models more powerful than the ones they already have. They argue the race creates a public risk; for now it is only a lawsuit and no court order has been issued.
per_que_importa: For the first time, a court is being asked to cap how powerful AI can get. Even if it fails, it shows that pressure to regulate these companies no longer comes only from governments but also from civil society.

titular: Mirendil, founded by former Anthropic researchers, raises $1bn in its first big round
resum: The San Francisco start-up has raised $1bn in a round led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital, with Google among the investors. It wants AI agents to do the work of an entire research lab; the company says a single researcher working with agents trained its coding model in three and a half months, a claim nobody has verified yet.
per_que_importa: A company less than a year old raising this much money shows how heavily investors are betting on AI that works on its own. If it works, research could move much faster; if not, it is a sign of how high expectations are.

titular: LangChain, which helps manage AI agents, is now worth $3bn
resum: LangChain has raised $300m in a round led by CapitalG, Alphabet's fund, valuing it at $3bn, more than double the $1.25bn of a year ago. Its LangSmith platform has 7,000 business customers.
per_que_importa: Companies using AI agents need tools to monitor what they do and prevent mistakes. This 'picks and shovels' business is growing as fast as AI itself and is creating new technical jobs.
xifra_text: LangChain's valuation, more than double a year ago

titular: OpenAI unveils AI agents that attack websites to find their security holes
resum: OpenAI has launched Daybreak Red Team, agents that test web applications and confirm security flaws, for now in early access by application. It comes with Defense Factory, in preview, which suggests how to fix the code; OpenAI has published neither prices nor test results.
per_que_importa: Cyberattacks cost businesses and governments a lot of money, and there aren't enough specialists. If AI can find holes before criminals do, security improves; but the same tools could also be used to attack.

titular: Nvidia drops below $4 trillion in value for the first time since July 2025
resum: New development: Nvidia shares fell another 2.01% on Friday, the day after Jensen Huang's resignation, and the company closed below $4 trillion in stock market value. The stock is down more than 20% in a month, ahead of Tuesday's results.
per_que_importa: Nvidia carries a lot of weight in the indices that many pension funds track, so its fall takes value away from many people's savings. It is also a gauge of confidence in the AI business.
xifra_text: Nvidia's drop on Friday, taking it below $4 trillion

titular: Australia's Q-CTRL raises $290m to make quantum computers work better
resum: Sydney-based Q-CTRL has closed a $290m funding round. The company makes software that reduces errors in quantum computers, one of the main barriers to this technology becoming useful.
per_que_importa: Quantum computers could speed up the design of new medicines or materials, but today they make too many mistakes. Investment in this field suggests investors believe real-world uses could arrive within a few years.

titular: ASUS unveils Gallop, its first humanoid robot, which is learning to pack in a factory
resum: The Taiwanese computer maker is training Gallop to pack motherboard accessories, aiming for a 99.5% success rate at 20 seconds per board, a human pace. It plans customer trials in 2027 and sales from 2028.
per_que_importa: ASUS says the robot isn't meant to replace workers but to take on repetitive, physically demanding jobs that are hard to fill. Big electronics makers joining in shows humanoids are starting to move from labs to factories.

titular: GXO could put up to 1,000 humanoid robots in its warehouses
resum: Logistics giant GXO has signed a letter of intent with Apptronik to expand trials of the Apollo robot, with the possibility of reaching 1,000 units over four years. It is not a firm order: each robot will have to earn its place in real-world trials starting in 2027.
per_que_importa: Warehouses are one of the first places where humanoids can do useful work, such as picking and packing orders. If the trials succeed, it will change how thousands of people work in logistics.
